Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'link the lamps.' Outside the book title, records use the phrase for succession from one Chan teacher or generation to another. A history of Drum Mountain says that from the founding of Xingsheng, 'the linked lamps were unbroken for more than seventy generations' (聯燈不絕，七十餘代), and later describes 'those who linked the lamps and continued the flame for more than seventy generations' (聯燈續焰者七十餘代). Memorial words say, 'continue the flame, link the lamp—the Way is not alone' (續燄聯燈道不孤); another memorial says two teachers later 'linked lamps, each in a different region' (聯燈各一方). An ancestral-hall address speaks of 'one portrait, in succession linking the lamp far away' (一㡧次第聯燈遠). The lamp image is defined in the same record: the Chan houses' transmission through successive generations is compared to a lamp because it breaks darkness and shows things, and because its illumination can be continued without end.
Senses.Note: The corpus contains 104 occurrences of the graphs in 28 allowed texts, but 77 occurrences in 13 texts belong to the proper title 'Linked-Lamp Essentials' (聯燈會要). This primary sense records the free verb/noun phrase in temple histories, memorials, and ancestral-hall addresses. Its recurring partner is 'continue the flame' (續燄／續焰).

Senses.Explanation: A proper-title and record-name use, chiefly within 'Linked-Lamp Essentials' (聯燈會要). Its own preface says that more than six hundred teachers were selected, their encounters, questions and answers, comments on old cases, and essential statements arranged under each person's chapter, divided into thirty fascicles, and 'named Linked-Lamp Essentials' (命曰聯燈會要). Another preface says the work was designated by that title and carved for circulation. Later histories place the linked-lamp work among the five lamp records: Transmission of the Lamp, Expanded Lamp, Continued Lamp, Linked Lamp, and Universal Lamp. Biographical notices say that Huiweng Wuming compiled the Linked-Lamp Essentials and transmitted it in Chan communities or circulated it in the world.
Senses.Note: This sense is separate because the graphs form a proper title or abbreviated record name rather than a predicate of lineage continuation. The full title 'Linked-Lamp Essentials' (聯燈會要) occurs 77 times in 13 allowed texts; the shorter title 'Linked-Lamp Record' (聯燈錄) occurs once.

Senses.Explanation: A considerable duration: “a good while.” The headword occurs 11,566 times across 387 allowlisted texts. In dialogue and hall addresses it is often rendered “after a long pause”: a master says nothing and then speaks, shouts, raises the fly-whisk, plants the staff, or steps down. A monk can also be the one who pauses, so the word does not itself encode a master's authoritative silence. The interval may be an entire assembly's unanswered wait: after the master asks whether anyone has a question, no one asks for a good while and he leaves. The pause may also constitute the whole recorded answer, as when a monk asks the master to say it directly and responds after the master's silence. Chan records repeatedly deploy the World-Honored One in this mode when a non-Buddhist asks about neither the spoken nor the unspoken. They also deploy Kāśyapa ascending the seat before King Ajātaśatru, waiting a good while, and descending without preaching. Elsewhere the headword marks ordinary elapsed narrative time before a summons and reply. All of these denote the same interval; the entry records its duration without assigning the silence an unstated meaning.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide temporal sense. Held silence in dialogue is the dominant Chan deployment, not part of the denotation in every occurrence. The curated passages include a monk's pause, an assembly's unanswered wait for questions, pauses followed by a whisk or staff gesture, the World-Honored One and Kāśyapa seat cases, and ordinary elapsed narrative time. Raised cases and generic dialogue frames keep null speaker fields.

AlternateTargets: after a long while, he said
Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'after a good while, said.' This fixed narrative formula occurs 2,037 times in 79 allowed texts. It marks an interval before quoted speech in dialogues and assembly addresses. In the Five Lamps Complete Collection, Tianyi Yihuai asks, 'Then what is it?' and after a while says, 'Do you understand? Take care!' (且作麼生即是？良久曰：還會麼？珍重). In a Five Lamps Rigorous Continuation address, the speaker ascends the hall, waits, says, 'Assembly, look, look,' and descends (上堂，良久曰：大眾看看。便下座). Another record asks where Maitreya is and, after a while, answers, 'When walking at night do not tread on white; if it is not water, it is stone' (且道彌勒在甚麼處？良久曰：夜行莫踏白，不是水便是石). The Continued Transmission of the Lamp supplies both extended statements and short closings after the formula: 'a drop of spring rain is slick as oil' (春雨一滴滑如油) and 'fine food does not suit a full person,' followed by descent from the seat (美食不中飽人喫。便下座). The punctuation varies by edition, but the sequence remains interval, speech verb, and quotation.
Senses.Note: The close variant 'after a while, said' with the alternate speech graph (良久云) occurs 1,403 times in 169 texts. 'Silently for a long while' (默然良久) occurs 45 times in 32 texts, while three records have 'after a while, descended from the seat' (良久下座) without the speech verb. Those forms confirm the components but are not merged into the headword count. No self-definition formula is applicable to this narrative connector.
